accept: old crumbly cork
fragile corks old bottles
~old or fragile
~fragile cork
~fragile corks
~fragile or crumbling
ans: The cork is old or fragile — prongs grip the sides without piercing
exp: The Durand combines worm and prongs for the truly ancient.

accept: heating neck then cold shock cracks glass clean
red-hot tongs plus wet cloth crack the neck
ans: Heating the neck red-hot, then a cold damp cloth — thermal shock parts the glass cleanly below a fused cork
exp: Theater plus function for decades-old Vintage Port.

q: Wine-by-the-glass preservation systems rank (name two with mechanisms):
accept: coravin argon needle vacuum pump nitrogen blanket
argon systems coravin vacuum inert gas
ans: Coravin (argon through the cork, cork never pulled), inert-gas blankets (argon/nitrogen), vacuum pumps (weakest)
exp: Know service-life claims: Coravin weeks-months, gas days, vacuum a day or two.

q: Correct glass-marking etiquette when pouring a comparative flight:
accept: pour left to right announce each wine position
consistent placement narrate order
ans: Consistent placement (left-to-right from the guest's view), announcing each wine as poured
exp: The Advanced practical grades your narration as much as your hands.

q: A guest insists a sound wine is corked. The Advanced-level response:
accept: replace graciously taste later manage host
take it back offer alternative without argument
ans: Replace it graciously without debate, verify away from the table, and note it for inventory — hospitality first, autopsy later
exp: You may gently educate only if the guest invites it.

q: Match the service temperature to the wine.
accept: match
ans: Fino–coldest · Vintage Champagne–cellar-cool · Barolo–cool room · Tawny–lightly chilled
exp: Vintage fizz warmer than NV: complexity over refreshment.

q: The sommelier's taste (when offered by the host) is properly:
accept: small pour tasted at gueridon
tiny pour away from table with thanks
ans: A small pour assessed briskly at the guéridon with thanks — confirming soundness, not savoring
exp: Some houses use a tastevin ceremonially; never linger.

q: BYO/corkage etiquette for the somm includes:
accept: treat as own list full service check policy no competing bottle
full service same care policy fee waived if buying
ans: Full standard service, house policy stated kindly, and the classic courtesy: waive fees when the table also buys from the list
exp: The bottle's provenance conversation can win a regular for life.

q: Sabrage strikes which seam of the bottle?
accept: the seam meeting the lip annulus
side seam to collar
ans: Along a side seam into the lip collar — the glass's weakest joint
exp: Cold bottle, firm follow-through, aimed away from everything living. Not an exam requirement — a party trick with liability.

q: The order of a formal multi-wine dinner service follows which principles?
accept: light before full dry before sweet young before old white before red with exceptions
ascending weight dry to sweet modest to grand
ans: Light before full, dry before sweet, young before old (grandest last) — menu logic may override dogma
exp: Sherry with consommé and Sauternes mid-meal with foie are honored exceptions.

q: A bottle lands at $40 a unit. Your program targets a 33% beverage cost. The list price is closest to:
exp: Cost divided by target cost percentage: 40 ÷ 0.33 is about 120, a three-times multiple. Doubling to $80 is a 50% cost, which cannot carry the labour and breakage a wine program actually incurs; five times at $200 is a 20% cost few guests will accept on a $40 bottle. Real programs blend rather than apply one multiple: aggressive markups on inexpensive by-the-glass, and thin percentage margins or a fixed dollar margin at the top so trophy bottles actually sell instead of decorating the list. A 30% blended cost with high turns beats a 22% cost on stock that never moves.

q: A guest orders a 1959 Bordeaux from your reserve list. Describe how you read the fill level, and what you say to the table before you open it.
accept: into neck bottom neck top shoulder upper shoulder mid shoulder low shoulder
read the ullage against the shoulder and warn the guest before the cork comes out
top shoulder is normal for a 1959 and mid shoulder is a real risk
show the fill and agree the sold as is conversation before opening
ans: Fill is read against the neck and shoulder: into neck or bottom neck is exceptional at that age, very top or top shoulder is normal for a 1950s wine, upper to mid shoulder is drinkable but a genuine risk, and low shoulder is a gamble. Older and Burgundy-shaped bottles are often quoted instead in centimetres measured from the base of the cork. I show the guest the fill, the capsule and any seepage, note the condition on the check, say plainly that a bottle of this age is sold as it stands unless it is faulty, and offer to open it at the table so we assess it together — with an alternative already chosen in case it has gone.
exp: Ullage is evaporation past the cork and therefore a proxy for how the bottle was stored; mid-shoulder in a 1959 usually means heat, and heat means a wine that fades in the glass within minutes of pouring. The commercial point is the sequence: the conversation you have before the cork comes out is a courtesy, and the identical conversation afterwards is a negotiation. Auction-condition vocabulary is Advanced currency because reserve lists are now sourced at auction.

q: Give the mechanics of opening Champagne correctly, including the pressure you are containing and the two habits that cause accidents.
accept: thumb stays on the cork and you turn the bottle not the cork about six atmospheres
hold at forty five degrees ease the cork out with a sigh roughly ninety psi
never let go of the cork and never open the bottle upright six bar of pressure
turn the bottle against a held cork keeping the cage on until the end
ans: Chill it properly, because cold wine holds its gas. A thumb goes on the cork the moment the foil is cut and does not leave until the cork is in your hand. Six half-turns loosen the wire, which stays on the cork. Hold the bottle at roughly forty-five degrees, aimed at nobody, grip the cork and turn the bottle rather than the cork, easing the cork against the thumb so it sighs instead of popping. You are containing about six atmospheres, near ninety psi. The two habits that hurt people are releasing the cork to reach for a napkin or to lift the cage off, and opening the bottle standing upright, which gives the cork a straight line to somebody's face.
exp: The angle is not only about aim: tilting the bottle increases the surface area between wine and gas, which lowers the chance of a gush and saves the pour. The sigh rather than the pop is not mere decorum either — a violent release costs mousse and throws foam. Keep the cage on while loosening, and remember the pressure figure, because 'about six atmospheres' is the answer that explains why every one of these habits exists.

q: Two bottles come back to the pass: one smells of damp cardboard, the other of struck match and drains. Separate them, and give the floor action for each.
accept: tca does not blow off so replace it while reduction clears with aggressive decanting
damp cardboard is cork taint struck match is reduction which aerates away
cork taint replace and claim reduction decant splash and retaste
trichloroanisole strips the fruit sulfides dissipate with air
ans: The first is cork taint — TCA, detectable in the low nanograms per litre, single-figure parts per trillion. It does not blow off; it strips fruit and grows duller with air. That bottle is finished: replace it, log it, claim it from the supplier. The second is reduction, volatile sulfur compounds thrown by a low-oxygen winemaking style. That does dissipate: decant hard, splash it, give it ten minutes, and if the aroma lifts and fruit arrives the wine is sound — but I taste it again myself before it goes back to the guest. Copper is a cellar remedy, not a floor one, and the clean-coin trick is folklore. If either call is genuinely in doubt, the guest wins.
exp: The commonest miss is not the mouldy bottle but the mild one: low-level TCA rarely smells of cardboard, it simply makes a wine flat, short and mute, and it gets sent back as 'boring' rather than faulty. Threshold figures usually quoted are 1.5 to 4 ng/L, with some tasters well below that. A reduction that returns after decanting is a bottle to withdraw from service, not one to keep airing at the table.

q: The ISO 3591 tasting glass, the reference glass for exams and competitions, is specified as:
exp: 215 ml total capacity, a 50 ml sample: a tulip bowl on a short stem, tapering to a narrow rim so aromatics concentrate identically for every taster in the room. The glass exists to standardise, not to flatter — it is deliberately unremarkable, and a Zalto or a varietal Riedel will show almost any wine better. That is exactly why it is the reference: a glass that improves a wine is a variable, and comparative tasting has enough of those already.

q: A regular you like is visibly intoxicated and orders another bottle in front of his guests. Handle it.
accept: cut him off discreetly away from the table and bring the manager in
stop the sale offer food water and a car then document it
refuse further service privately protecting the guest's face and the licence
dram shop liability means the house stops serving and arranges transport
ans: I stop the sale, and I do it without an audience. I catch the host away from the table or bend to him quietly, tell him warmly that we are going to pause the wine and bring food and water, and steer him toward coffee or something that arrives without alcohol. I never announce the refusal to the table and I never leave a server holding it — the manager comes in and the house owns the decision. I offer to hold the bottle for his next visit, which lets him keep face and keeps the sale, and I arrange a car. Then I document it: the time, what was served, what we did. In most jurisdictions the licence-holder carries liability for serving a visibly intoxicated guest and for what he does after he leaves, and the licence is the restaurant's life.
exp: Over-service is the one hospitality decision in which the guest does not win, and the Advanced examiners want to hear you say so without flinching. The practical craft is in the replacement: a bare 'no' produces an argument, while 'no' arriving with food, water, a held bottle and a car gets accepted almost every time. Liability rules differ by jurisdiction — know yours, and know that documentation written that night is worth more than memory a year later.
